title: LibriBrain100: 100 Hours of MEG Data for Neural Speech Decoding
hook: Most brain-decoding datasets go wide across many subjects. This one goes deep — ~80 hours inside a single brain — to test whether depth beats breadth.
key_points: Over 100 hours of MEG recorded while subjects listened to naturalistic continuous speech.
~80 hours come from one subject — the authors report 8x more within-subject data than the next comparable set.
Deep single-subject data plus an existing decoder set a new state of the art on a word-classification benchmark.
Adds ~40 minutes each from 32 more subjects to test the practical case of little data per user.
Finetuning a pre-trained model on that broad data substantially compensates for thin per-subject recordings.
Ships fixed train/val/test splits, an open Python loader, and a public-leaderboard competition.
content_html: Non-invasive brain-to-text decoding — reading intended or heard speech from sensors outside the skull — has been held back less by models than by data. MEG recordings are expensive, and most datasets sample a little from many people. LibriBrain100, from Oiwi Parker Jones's group and collaborators (arXiv, August 2026), inverts that: over 100 hours of MEG collected while subjects listened to naturalistic continuous speech, with roughly 80 of those hours from a single subject — by the authors' count, 8x more within-subject data than the next comparable dataset.
extra_html:
The payoff they report is on a word-classification benchmark, an intermediate step toward full brain-to-text: feeding an existing decoding model this much within-subject data yields state-of-the-art performance, which they read as validating both recording quality and the value of depth. Because nobody will sit through 80 hours of scanning to use a real device, they also recorded about 40 minutes from each of 32 additional subjects and show that supervised finetuning of a pre-trained model substantially closes the gap when per-subject data is scarce — the transfer-learning story that would make consumer BCIs plausible.

The release includes standard train/validation/test splits, an open-source Python library for downloading and loading the data into common frameworks, and an accompanying machine-learning competition with a public leaderboard. See the paper for details and the benchmark definition.

related.title: The Pile: 800GB of Diverse Text
related.hook: Web text alone leaves gaps. The Pile stitches together 22 curated sources — academic and professional — so a language model picks up knowledge plain web crawls miss.

flashcards.back_html: Instead of spreading recording time thinly across many people, it concentrates ~80 of its 100+ hours in a single subject — testing what a lot of data from one brain buys you.

flashcards.prompt: Why did the authors also collect ~40 minutes each from 32 extra subjects?

choices.text: Because 80 hours per user is impractical in the real world, so they test whether broad multi-subject pretraining can substitute
To act as a held-out test set for the single-subject model
To measure how MEG hardware drifts between sessions

flashcards.explanation_html: Real deployments get minutes, not days, per person. The broad cohort lets them show that finetuning a pre-trained model largely compensates for limited per-subject data.

flashcards.prompt: Why do standard splits and an open loader matter as much as the recordings?
flashcards.back_html: They make results comparable. Neural decoding papers often use bespoke preprocessing and splits, so fixed splits plus a public leaderboard turn scattered claims into a shared benchmark.
